summary: This program demonstrates Java's four levels of method access — public, protected, package-private, and private — using the analogy of sharing a message with different-sized audiences. All four methods are called from main inside the same class, which is the one place every access level is allowed.

lines.text: The class itself is public, so any other class in the program can refer to it. The file must be named ShareMessageModifiers.java to match.
This is the entry point Java looks for when you run the class, so execution begins here.
The four sharing methods are instance methods, not static ones, so you need an object to call them on. This creates one and names it demo.
Calling the public method works from here and would work equally well from any other class in any package.
The protected method is reachable from the same package or from a subclass, and code inside the class itself always qualifies.
The package-private method has no modifier at all, so only classes sitting in the same package may call it.
The private method can only be called from inside ShareMessageModifiers, which is exactly where this line lives. Moving this call to another class would cause a compile error.
public is the widest setting: no restriction on who may call the method.
protected narrows access to the same package plus subclasses, even subclasses declared in a different package.
Leaving off the modifier entirely gives package-private access, the default when you say nothing. It is narrower than protected because subclasses in other packages are shut out.
private is the narrowest setting and the one to reach for by default, because it keeps helper logic hidden inside the class that owns it.
